sketches: If every finite family F containing a forest is k-nice for all k ≥ k0(F) (Question 1.1), then in particular it is k-nice for infinitely many k. The paper itself poses the conjecture as 'a weaker version of Question 1.1'.
If F is k-nice for all k >= k0(F), then it is k-nice for infinitely many k; the paper poses the target as the weaker version of the source question.

source.name: Forest families eventually k-nice
source.statement: Is it true that for any finite family of graphs $\mathcal{F}$ that contains at least one forest, there exists a constant $k_0 = k_0(\mathcal{F})$ such that $\mathcal{F}$ is $k$-nice for all $k \geq k_0$?
source.context: It is easy to see that if $\mathcal{F}$ contains no forest then it is not $k$-nice for any $k$. The question asks whether a converse holds: every family containing at least one forest is eventually $k$-nice. The paper proves this for all families containing a graph with at most 2 edges and for several two-graph families of 3-edge connected graphs.

target.name: Forest-containing families are infinitely k-nice
target.statement: Any finite family of graphs $\mathcal{F}$ that contains at least one forest is $k$-nice for infinitely many integers $k$.
target.context: This is posed as a weaker version of Question 1.1. Theorem 1.4 shows that $\mathcal{F}_7 = \{K_3, P_4, S_3\}$ is $k$-nice for infinitely many $k$, and Theorem 1.6 gives further support for families containing a star $K_{1,r+1}$.

sketches: Graphs embeddable in a fixed surface of genus g form a proper minor-closed family (genus is minor-monotone and some graph has larger genus). So the linear bound xc(P_sp.trees(G))=O(|V|) for all proper minor-closed families restricts to the bounded-genus conjecture; the paper introduces Conjecture 2 as the generalization of Conjecture 1.

Graphs embeddable in a fixed surface form a proper minor-closed family, so the O(|V|) spanning-tree-polytope extension-complexity conjecture for minor-closed families contains the fixed-surface version as a special case.

source.name: Linear extension complexity for minor-closed families
source.statement: If $\mathcal{C}$ is a proper minor-closed family of graphs and $G = (V, E)$ is a connected graph in $\mathcal{C}$, then $\mathrm{xc}(P_{\mathrm{sp.trees}}(G)) = O(|V|)$.
source.context: Following Conjecture 1, the authors suggest the linear bound may hold even more generally for all proper minor-closed families. They note the conjecture is known to hold when graphs in $\mathcal{C}$ have bounded treewidth, and they prove it for $k$-apex graphs (Theorem 4) as additional supporting evidence.

target.name: Linear xc bound for bounded-genus spanning trees
target.statement: If $G = (V, E)$ is a connected graph embedded in a fixed surface, then $\mathrm{xc}(P_{\mathrm{sp.trees}}(G)) = O(|V|)$.
target.context: The authors prove an $O(g^{1/2}|V|^{3/2} + g^{3/2}|V|^{1/2})$ upper bound for graphs embedded in a surface of genus $g$ (Theorem 3). They conjecture that this can be improved to match the linear bound known for planar graphs (Theorem 2, due to Williams).

sketches: The conjecture that the induced arithmetic removal lemma (Theorem 1.14) holds for arbitrary Z-coefficient patterns over arbitrary abelian groups is precisely the proposed resolution of the open problem of extending the lemma beyond complexity-1 patterns over F_q to higher complexity and general abelian groups (including Z); its truth settles both extensions asked for.

source.name: Induced arithmetic removal over abelian groups
source.statement: A statement analogous to Theorem 1.14 holds for arbitrary patterns with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}$ over arbitrary abelian groups, subject to appropriate caveats concerning infinite complexity patterns and trivial solutions.
source.context: Immediately following the statement of the main theorem (Theorem 1.14) and its remark on tower-type bounds, the authors write: 'We conjecture that a similar statement holds for arbitrary patterns (with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}$) in arbitrary abelian groups.' They decline to give a precise formulation due to unresolved issues with infinite complexity and trivial solutions.

target.name: Induced arithmetic removal for higher complexity patterns
target.statement: Extend the induced arithmetic removal lemma beyond complexity 1 patterns over finite fields to higher complexity patterns and to general abelian groups (even the case of $\mathbb{Z}$ is open).
target.context: After establishing Theorem 1.14 for complexity 1 patterns over $\mathbb{F}_q$, the authors note that extending to higher complexity and to general groups remains open. They observe that for affine-invariant patterns (which avoid a regularisation difficulty near the origin), the problem for bounded complexity patterns over finite fields has been solved, but the general induced setting is still unresolved.

sketches: Problem 1.10 (is f(d)/f_{≤2}(d) subexponential in n=2^{d-1}?) is exactly part (iii) of Problem 1.2, which asks for the order of magnitude of the four ratios and which of them is exponential in n; the paper's own context says Problem 1.10 'addresses Problem 1.2 (iii)'. Determining the order of magnitude of ratio (iii) answers the subexponentiality question.

source.name: Hypercube partition ratio growth rates
source.statement:
What is the order of magnitude of the
following ratios? In particular, which one of them is an
exponential function of $n$? 
(i) $m^{\prime}(d)/m(d)$,   (ii) $f_{\leq 2}(d)/m^{\prime}(d)$,
  (iii) $f(d)/f_{\leq 2}(d),$    (iv) $f(d)/m(d)$.
source.context: The hierarchy $m(d) \leq m^{\prime}(d) \leq f_{\leq 2}(d) \leq f(d)$ holds by definition, where $n = 2^{d-1}$. The paper proves that $f(d)/m(d)$ (part iv) is exponential in $n$, and shows part (i) is subexponential; parts (ii) and (iii) remain open.

target.name: Subexponential gap for dimension-2 subcube partitions
target.statement:
Is it true that
$f(d)/f_{\leq 2}(d)$ is subexponential in $n$?
target.context: This addresses Problem 1.2 (iii), asking whether the gap between counting all subcube partitions and counting those restricted to subcubes of dimension at most 2 grows at most subexponentially in $n = 2^{d-1}$.
